content.text: {"relation":"MATCH","consensus_summary":"The blind consensus holds that the door/gate primarily symbolizes access to God and salvation, with Christ himself as the exclusive door through which believers enter eternal life and the fold of God (John 10:7-9; Matt 7:13-14). Secondary contextual uses include open doors of ministry opportunity, the door of the heart, gates as civic power/authority, eschatological shut doors, and typological OT doors (Passover doorposts, ark, tabernacle).","book_summary":"The book defines the door/gate as the destination of the way — the entrance into the house of God, marked on the posts — citing the Passover blood on the doorposts (Ex 12:7), the commanded writing on posts and gates (Deut 6:9), and Christ's declaration 'I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved' (John 10:9).","consensus_core_identification":"The door/gate is the point of access to God and salvation, identified supremely with Christ as the one entrance (John 10:9).","book_core_identification":"The door is the entrance into God's house — the terminus of the way — identified with Christ (John 10:9) and prefigured by the marked doorposts of Passover and the Shema.","core_relation":"EQUIVALENT","extension_relation":"SAME_CASES","boundary_disagreement":"None material. The book foregrounds the Passover/Deuteronomy doorpost-marking typology, which the consensus lists as a minority alternative, and frames the door as 'the destination of the way' (an internal cross-reference to a 'way' motif). Neither move alters the central identification; the book simply omits the peripheral uses (open door of opportunity, civic gates, gates of Hades) that the consensus treats as context-specific secondary meanings, as glossary brevity would predict.","material_contradiction":"None. Both identify the door as the entrance to God/salvation with Christ as that door.","rationale":"Reduced to minimum cores, both readings say the same thing: the door symbolizes entrance into God's presence/salvation, and Christ is that door (John 10:9 is cited by both). The book's distinctive coloring — marked posts (Ex 12:7; Deut 6:9) and the door as the endpoint of 'the way' — is compatible elaboration already anticipated in the consensus's typological alternative (blood-marked doorposts prefiguring Christ) and in its pairing of the door saying with John 14:6 ('the way'). No cases are added, excluded, or reclassified at the level of the core identification, so this is MATCH rather than REFINED.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue REFINED because the book narrows the symbol to 'the entrance to the house of God marked on the posts,' elevating a Passover/Shema typology the consensus treats as minority, and reframing the door as the destination of a 'way' schema rather than simply access to salvation; this could be read as a material reweighting of the symbol's center. But since the consensus's central referent (Christ as the saving entrance, John 10:9) is fully retained and explicitly cited, the reweighting is emphasis, not boundary change.","confidence":"high"}
